$comment: THE STAGE TABLE — the one place a stage's status is recorded.
`scripts/docs.test.mjs` reads this file. Two rules make it more than a list:
1. A stage may not be `shipped` while any `DEFER(engine-N)` marker in the
tree names it. A stage table that has started lying is worse than none,
because it is re-read and believed by somebody with no memory.
2. Every guard's `stage` names a row here, so a guard cannot protect work
that is not on the map.
`ends` is the exit criterion — an observable, not a feeling. It is what makes
`shipped` a claim somebody could check rather than a decision somebody made.

stages.title: Ground — workspace, docs, guard registry, standards
Kernel — entities, declarations, gate algebra, problems
Directory + placement
Runtime — manifest → live worker
Identity + tenancy
Surface — HeroUI shell, nav, sky, rendered settings
Money — plans, entitlements, credits, jobs
Services — ai and notify over RPC
Vault + legal
A real product on OneEngine, end to end
One — the deployment and the OneSpace
The agent surface — every operation an MCP tool, derived
Multi-app access — a platform role for the workspace, a role per app inside it
The package rail — a priced bundle of timed grants, one ledger, one clock
The tenant centre — the shell with the router: five areas + app screens inside
The operator console — the same shell on `admin.`, and the maintenance switch
AI actions — a lane per action, a model the operator binds, words that narrow
OneSpace — one surface over the product, reachable from every door, addressed
OneDesign — the design system named, packaged, documented and fenced
Workspaces — personal or commercial, one brand, one installable, a shard of their own
Payment — a workspace subscribes, and only a signed event stamps the plan
OneSpace — `id`, `admin` and `setup` merge into one address off the workspace root
Mail that leaves the process — a letter, its variables, and a provider
A workspace composes its own roles out of one app's keys
stages.ends: `custom_role` was applied, read by `permissionsFor` and written by nothing — a table, a resolver and a refusal rule with no way to reach any of them. `role.list`, `role.save` and `role.remove` are the three that make it real. `beyond_you` is the one to read twice: a workspace composing a role out of keys its author does not hold is the shortest path from “I can manage people” to “I can do anything” — make the role, assign it to yourself — and `saveRole` is the only writer that reaches the check. A role somebody still holds may not be deleted: the registry would stop carrying it, `permissionsFor` would resolve it to nothing, and they would keep their seat and be able to do nothing at all with no screen saying why.

stages.title: Agreements — versioned documents, an acceptance per person per version, and the wall until there is one
The vault is opened — consent, who looked, your data, and an erasure that shreds
The AI lane runs — a catalogue that syncs itself, one door out to every provider, a charge built on what the call really cost, and a nightly check against the bill we are sent
Notifications are filed — an event raised becomes a note in somebody's inbox
The daily sweep — erasure happens on a clock, and every run is recorded
A workspace's apps are turned on and off, and a workspace can move shard
Account security — sign out everywhere, and proving it is you again before something irreversible
A manifest changes while the deployment is up, and the composed surface forgets
A guard refuses a declared setting nothing names — the seam a handler reads one through is live; the completeness check over it is not
The kernel's remaining conveniences are each used by a lane or removed
A workspace runs its own retention ladder against its own customers, and ours freezes it
The deployment provisions itself — a product declares what it needs underneath it, and the reconciler makes it exist in the right jurisdiction, binds it, and reaps it after a drain
A workspace's records change shard, which is the only way its jurisdiction can — read-only while it copies, verified before it flips, and the source drained rather than emptied

A notification leaves the process — Web Push written out rather than depended on, a subscription filed under the door it was made at so it wears that workspace's own icon, and a keypair the console generates and never accepts
The documentation is two generated pages — what exists, derived from the engine; and how to add to it, which no generator can derive
An app ships a screen — a product's browser half is a chunk of its own, loaded when its workspace opens it, drawing that workspace's own records through the door it is handed
A workspace's brand reaches the screen — the surfaces it picked, and only the ones its products have
stages.ends: A workspace's brand reaches the two surfaces the deployment actually has, and only where the workspace asked for them. The editor stored the picks and NOTHING read them: the tile was painted from `mayBrand` alone — so a business that turned `app-icons` off still installed as itself — and no screen wore the theme at all. Being entitled to brand and asking to brand HERE are two questions, and reading only the first is what made every switch on that screen save and change nothing. `centre.view` now answers with the theme or with nothing, and `paintFor` reads the pick; the intersection is resolved where the surface is SERVED rather than where it is drawn, because every screen deciding for itself is how one product ends up branded and the next one beside it is not. On the page it is a second style element appended after the boot's — at equal specificity source order decides, and absent means EMPTY rather than untouched, or the last workspace's colours survive a switch.

stages.title: A screen asks the gate before it draws a control, rather than after it is pressed
stages.ends: `blockedBy` was declared in the kernel and called by nothing, so a control the gate would refuse was drawn, pressed, and failed — the refusal arriving as a toast over a form somebody had already filled in. The Ask is now built ONCE per request and asked twice: for this request's own gate, and for what else this caller could do. `centre.view` carries the second answer as `may`, only for what is BLOCKED (absent means allowed, which is also where a client that forgets the field lands), and every input is settled in memory by the locator so fifty operations cost fifty pure walks and no query. On the page it arrives through a CONTEXT rather than a prop — a prop is a thing every screen in every product has to remember to pass, and the one that forgets is not visibly different. An act names the OPERATION it calls rather than a verdict, so a screen never restates the gate's question in its own words; `Screen`'s primary and `Confirm`'s act both read it, and the words per gate are the design system's (`STOPPED`) rather than each screen's.

stages.title: The proving ground's remaining screens reach a workspace's own records
stages.ends: nothing — D52 made the ground a fixture with no `live` entry, so there is no workspace whose records it could reach, and `scripts/fixture.test.mjs` refuses the entry back

stages.title: A one-off purchase — a credit pack, and becoming a business — through the same checkout
A plan is edited from the console, and everybody already on it keeps what they were sold
The wallet tops itself up — a standing instruction, a cooldown, and a decline the customer can read
Storage is metered rather than refused — the included amount is where the meter starts, and an empty wallet costs the writes and never the files
The deployment's legal identity is complete — the registered address it is written to, and whether selling where it sells needs a representative there
stages.ends: `IDENTITY.address` is the address on the licence rather than the Emirate, and either a representative is declared beside the sub-processors or a written decision says none is needed for where this deployment sells

stages.title: A stranger joins a workspace by themselves — a door the workspace opens, a role the app names, and a ceiling the plan sells (D23)
stages.ends: an app declares `access.joining`, composition refuses a joining role that is not a customer or that reads a tenant-scoped collection, `me.join` resolves its workspace from the door, and the customer ceiling refuses with a sentence naming the upgrade

stages.title: The interface speaks a second language — dictionaries, a language control, and the copy guard reading both
stages.ends: `Presentation.language` is offered on the Formats screen, every written string in `@engine/design` and `engine/one-space` resolves through a dictionary, and `tone.test.mjs` checks the voice in each language rather than only in English

stages.title: A collection says `searchable` and becomes findable — the write marks, a pass carries, erasure removes, and one filter is the boundary
stages.ends: `searchable` on a `CollectionSpec` produces the ledger, the `<collection>.search` operation, the quarter-hourly index pass and the removal on delete and on erasure, with `searching.test.mjs` making each of the four silences a test failure.

stages.title: The words arrive as they are written — one metered run, streamed, and the charge rides the last token
stages.ends: `ctx.stream` answers with an SSE `Response` from the same reserve, model and words `ctx.generate` uses; `generateStream` holds the same four bounds; a cancelled stream settles at the reserve and is corrected by the nightly check; `metering.test.mjs` asks the streaming lane every question it asks the other.

stages.title: A workspace asks to change its jurisdiction, and the ask is the only thing that is new
stages.ends: A workspace with `tenant:manage` can request a residency change from its own settings; the request is recorded and answered by an operator rather than granted, because Cloudflare fixes a database's jurisdiction at creation and the move is `op.tenant.move`'s `into` either way. `operator.test.mjs` sees the read behind the operator's queue of them, and nothing in the request path can begin a move by itself.

stages.title: A collection's `offline` policy reaches the browser — a write survives no signal, and a read answers without one
stages.ends: `offline` is read by the runtime and by the browser rather than only declared: `queue` holds a write until there is a connection and replays it once, `cache` answers a read from what was last seen and says how old it is, and `none` is honest about failing. `scripts/declared.test.mjs` fails on any field of a kernel declaration that no lane reads, which is the check that would have found this one.

stages.title: A collection narrows to part of a workspace — a location grant, and one filter the platform composes
stages.ends: `reach` on an `AppSpec` names the collection whose rows are the places and the field they nest by; `reachBy` on a collection names the field that says where one record is. A membership carries the places somebody works in, per app; a grant to a site covers everything under it, resolved at the read rather than frozen into the grant; and `null` — every membership until somebody is narrowed — is the whole workspace. The five generated verbs filter and refuse by themselves, `member.places` and `member.reach` are the roster's read and write, bounded by the granter's own reach, and `scripts/reach.test.mjs` fails on any statement over a narrowed table that neither carries the filter nor states why it is wide. The AUDIENCE of a notification is deliberately not narrowed — see `audienceFor`.

stages.title: A family takes a hue — one declared per product, never written at a call site
stages.ends: `tint` carries more than one hue, each declared once in `scene/tint.ts` as a constraint on the family, chosen by name rather than by value; `scene.test.mjs` still refuses a colour written into a screen; and two products wearing the family are visibly different and neither is nameable.

stages.title: Records move between workspaces — a garage becomes a business and its history goes with it
stages.ends: A workspace's records can be handed to another workspace the same account can already reach, with the ledger's provenance carried rather than restamped, refused where the destination's apps do not cover the source's collections, and audited on both sides. Until it exists the only path is an export and an import, which loses who did what and when.

stages.title: An operation's ceiling is in force — calls per minute, per caller, refused rather than declared
stages.ends: `OperationSpec.rate` is read inside `performOperation`, so both doors obey it and neither can forget; a caller past the ceiling is refused with a catalogued problem naming when to try again; and the counter is bounded rather than a row per call.

stages.title: A write says it worked — the sentence the operation declared, and the reads it made stale
stages.ends: `OperationSpec.outcome` reaches the browser and is applied by the one door: a successful write raises its declared message in its declared tone exactly once, and every operation it names in `invalidates` is re-read rather than left showing what was true before the press.

stages.title: OneInventory exists — the model, the one chokepoint that moves a balance, and the arithmetic under both
stages.ends: The manifest composes and the deployment prices every key it declares; `product`, `location`, `stock` and `ledger` are collections with the balance and the history opted out of every generated write; `stock.receive`, `stock.take` and `stock.adjust` go through one function that writes the event and the projection in one batch and refuses rather than clamping; and `ledger-chokepoint.test.mjs` fails on a second place that writes either table.

stages.title: A product's screens reach each other — the route is the app's, the prefix is the platform's
stages.ends: A mounted screen is handed `go`, which takes the app's OWN route; `routeIn` adds the workspace prefix for the nav and for a row inside a screen alike, so the two are one address rather than two copies of one expression. Until it existed an app's list could not open the record it listed, and the only way it could have was by writing the centre's address scheme into a product.

stages.title: A list narrows and pages — the generated read answers past the first fifty, and says how many there are
stages.ends: The generated `list` takes a filter over declared fields, a cursor and a count. `where` is equality over what the collection declares — a comparison language would be a query language arriving over the wire, and equality answers “this shelf's lines”, which is what a screen asks. The cursor is `(at, id)` rather than an offset, because rows arrive at the TOP: an offset of fifty on a collection that gained three since the first page steps over three the reader has never seen, silently. And the total is the collection's, counted over the same `WHERE` and WITHOUT the cursor, so it does not fall as somebody reads — a page of fifty out of two hundred was indistinguishable from a collection of fifty, and the screen drawing it said “fifty products” with complete confidence. The count runs BESIDE the page rather than before it, so the latency budget's `depth` is unchanged and only its trip count moved, 11 → 12, on purpose.

stages.title: The guide and the milestones are ticked by what a workspace has actually done
stages.ends: A workspace's own tally — `tenant_event`, one row per (workspace, app, event), upserted on the way out of every successful operation that raises one — is what `guide.view` reads, so a step is ticked by what HAPPENED rather than by a screen deciding it looks done. Recorded beside `told` rather than inside it: the notification path returns early when an event has no audience, which is right for an inbox and wrong for a checklist. A milestone is said once and `tenant_milestone` is what stops it — `guide.seen` is a separate write, because a read that recorded the congratulation would spend it on a page somebody loaded and closed. And a step or milestone on an event only a JOB raises is refused at composition: the event exists, so the old check passed, and the step then sat unticked for ever because a sweep is not something anybody did.

stages.title: Itemised things — one object for its whole life, and the kits composed of them
stages.ends: `unit` and `kit` are collections nothing can write by hand; issuing, taking back and retiring an object each move the shelf through the same chokepoint a box of gloves does, and `item-life.test.mjs` fails on a standing changed without one. A kit is checked against the recipe it was ASSEMBLED under, a build is refused while anything is short and a stray is reported rather than refused, and taking anything out of a built kit un-builds it. Our own label is the only code in a workspace that names one object rather than a type, which is what lets a count say "you have already counted that one".

stages.title: A model can be shown something — the vision lane carries a picture, and the reserve counts it
stages.ends: `Ask.image` reaches the compat endpoint as a content part rather than being dropped, so `lane: "vision"` is a capability and not a name; `TOKENS_PER_IMAGE` puts the picture in the reserve, whether or not the units were counted by hand, because the settle cap makes an under-count permanently ours. And `ai-commits.test.mjs` fails on any operation that generates AND writes — a model fills anything, and a person commits.

stages.title: The release rail — a run ends, a person releases, and a late result may contradict neither
stages.ends: `process`, `process-item` and `job` are collections nothing writes by hand. Ending a run and releasing what it produced are separate acts under separate grants, because a green light is not a qualification. A quarantine freezes stock the chokepoint then REFUSES a take from, and lifts to needs-work — `release-ladder.test.mjs` fails on a release with no compare-and-set and on a lift that writes `released`. A late result that contradicts what is recorded is refused and names both facts; a late failure on a released run is a recall, which freezes what it can reach and NAMES what it cannot. And a job's trace is a query rather than a stored status, so a job correct on Tuesday acquires a concern on Thursday without anything about the job changing.

stages.title: A screen can be gated on an entitlement, the way an operation already is
stages.ends: `ScreenSpec.features` names the capabilities a screen is FOR, and the boot read withholds the screen unless the plan includes one of them — so a destination the workspace did not buy has no nav row, no route and no way in by typing, which is the same three answers a flag already gave. It is asked on the SERVER rather than in the chrome: the page holds no plan, and giving it one would be a second round trip on the read every screen stands on plus a second opinion about what was bought. ANY rather than ALL, because a page carrying runs and work orders is worth opening on a tier that has only work orders. Composition refuses a screen gated on a key nothing sells, and deliberately does NOT count a screen as enforcement — hiding a nav row leaves the operations behind it callable, so a key whose only mention is a screen is still sold and withheld by nothing.

stages.title: A night’s work can tell somebody — a job raises events, and the nightly sweep uses it
stages.ends: `JobCtx` carries `tell` and `setting`, so a per-tenant job reaches the same inbox a request does — the same audience-by-permission, the same channel resolution, the same workspace numbers — and `eventsOf` counts a job’s `emits`, so a notification about something nobody was present for composes. The runner refuses an undeclared event and `refuseJob` refuses `emits` on a deployment-scope job, because a note is filed in a workspace. OneInventory’s expiry sweep is the first: it tells about CROSSINGS rather than states — `crossedOn` is arithmetic, so nothing is remembered, a repeat run names the same batches, and nobody is told the same thing every morning for a month. `job-tells.test.mjs` fails on a job that declares an event and never raises it.

stages.title: Labels — a QR from nothing, a printable sheet, and the decant label a hazard needs
stages.ends: `@engine/design` draws a QR itself (ISO/IEC 18004, byte mode, level M, versions 1–10) — hand-written, and only defensible because `qr.test.ts` DECODES what it produces with a reader that shares no code with it: unmasks, reads the format bits back, de-interleaves, checks every Reed-Solomon syndrome is zero, parses the payload. One symbology for everything we print, because two encoders are two ways for a tag to come out unscannable. `LabelSheet`/`Label`/`LabelText` are the one place in the system measured in millimetres, because a label has a physical size and a screen does not. OneInventory declares a GHS classification on a product and prints the decant label a decanted bottle legally needs — signal word, hazards, statements verbatim — says plainly that the diamond is not the regulated pictogram, and reports a classification that contradicts itself where the label is printed rather than refusing it. Printing a place or a product MINTS its code, and `label-once.test.mjs` fails on any statement that could re-issue one.

stages.title: Reports — what went, what was wrong, what to buy, and how much of it anybody wrote down
stages.ends: Every figure is derived from the ledger and nothing is stored, because a correction made in March changes what February consumed and a stored number never learns that. One operation answers all four, so a screen cannot show a month’s usage beside a fortnight’s losses. The HERO is the recorded share — the number that makes the product look bad, and the only one that says whether the others mean anything. Short and over stay apart, because netting them off draws a shelf that is wildly wrong as a shelf that is fine. What to buy is ordered by what runs out FIRST against the workspace’s own lead time, never by what is smallest — which is how a store room runs out of the thing that takes a month to get. `inferred-consumption.test.mjs` fails if the id a count mints and the prefix the report reads ever drift apart, or if a close stops naming its session.

stages.title: The spreadsheet somebody already has — the import, and the supplier it names
stages.ends: Nobody types in eight hundred products, so a paste of a stock list is the difference between a trial and a workspace. Quotes are parsed rather than stripped, the separator is read off the heading and a European decimal is not a thousands separator — each of those is a catalogue that looks complete and is wrong. The mapping is GUESSED and then SHOWN, editable, because a guess that puts the supplier's name in the product name for eight hundred rows is only catchable before it happens; every refused row comes back with its line number and its reason rather than being dropped. `one-planner.test.mjs` fails if the preview and the commit ever stop being one function — two walks of one sheet agree until the day they do not, and on that day nothing throws. A supplier is the last step of the reorder report's own workflow: it can say what to buy and, without this, not who to ring — and its own lead time beats the workspace's, which is the slowest supplier a place has.

stages.title: An operation's declared input is checked at the door, and `now` is one type
stages.ends: `checkAll` was reached by collection records and by settings and by nothing else, so every operation's `input` map was a declaration the tool catalogue, the OpenAPI document and every generated form were written from, with nothing standing behind it — a required field could be absent, a four-hundred-thousand-character bound was advisory, and a `day` could be any string. The symptom was never a 400: the field arrived as `undefined`, reached a statement, and D1 answered `Type 'undefined' not supported` in a 503 naming a value rather than a field. It is checked before the handler now, it names the field, and the generated verbs stay exempt because `records.ts` owns create-versus-update. `Ctx.now` is a STRING, the same as `JobCtx.now` — one word had two types in one framework and the one an app can write to a row is the string. And a job's budget is wall-clock from the start of the pass rather than from the logical instant, which had made every run handed a past instant break before the first workspace and report a clean night. `input-checked.test.mjs` holds the door; all of it was found by making real requests to a real worker, which nothing in this repository had done for an app.

stages.title: The other half of OneInventory, driven — and the quarantine that was a badge on a screen
stages.ends: Deliveries and the two expiry clocks, itemised objects and their life, kits and their recipes, the release ladder and the nightly sweep are all executed against a real database through the real door now, in `inventory-deep.test.ts`. It found the one that matters most: loading something into a run did not HOLD it. `freeze` set `standing = 'held'` on a failed or recalled run — the states where somebody has already noticed — and nothing held what was merely waiting to be signed for. So a tray whose cycle had ended and which no qualified person had released could be taken off the shelf and used on somebody, while the screen showed "waiting to be released". The gap between a machine finishing and a person signing for what came out of it is what this product has instead of deciding that a green light is a qualification, and until this stage the gap was a label. `process.put` holds; `process.release` stamps `ok`; `process.lift` unfreezes one item with a reason; receiving more of a held lot stays possible, because a quarantine is about what may LEAVE.

stages.title: The foot of a phone is a vignette, and everywhere an app declares is reachable from it
stages.ends: `--hem-bottom` was written by nobody, so the bottom vignette fell to its default of 1 on every screen: fully opaque, with the world's marks stopping dead at its top edge, which is a bar by the definition the top hem's own paragraphs give. Both hems ask the same question now — is anything actually behind this — and the easing is armed a frame after the first answer so a screen that arrives with nothing behind its nav is drawn that way rather than fading out of a hem it never should have had. And `nav: "secondary"` was drawn in the desktop rail and nowhere else, so an app declaring twelve destinations offered five to a phone and seven had no gesture at all. The bar's fifth slot is the way to the rest: a destination rather than a menu, wearing the app's mark, opening to say WHICH place somebody is in when they are inside one. `phoneNav` is the split as one function so the invariant — every declared destination in exactly one of the two lists — is something a test can ask about, and `design/test/reachable.test.tsx` asks it. D46.

stages.title: A raw ALTER is a 503 on every door, and every standard page wears the curtain
stages.ends: `stampOf` is a content hash over a module's statements, so ANY edit to a module replays ALL of them — and `ALTER TABLE … ADD COLUMN` is the one statement that cannot be replayed. Three modules carried one; the first edit to any of them threw `duplicate column name` out of `boot`, which is upstream of the router, so every door on the deployment answered 503 and the identity screen said "One could not start". It is invisible on a fresh database, therefore green in every suite, and it took the live deployment down. `columns` already existed for exactly this — it is reconciled against the live table rather than executed — so the three moved onto it and `refuseSql` now refuses the word ALTER outright, which makes the next one a test failure at the point of writing. The other half is what somebody SEES when a deployment cannot answer: `Opening` is the only screen that draws while One is starting, and there were three more — a stopped boot, a host that is not a workspace, a route that is not a screen — each its own layout, drifting. `Opening` takes a `stopped` and draws all four, so the ring completes instead of turning and the message replaces the rotating line, on the same gradient with the same grain. `Elsewhere.tsx` is deleted; `Sheet` went with it, because a centred panel is a `Group` in a `Center` and the third way of saying so had no renderer. D47.

stages.title: A person is a subject, and an operator may give them things
stages.ends: The console could see every workspace and nobody in one, and every way of handing something out began by knowing a workspace — so "give my friend a workspace at the top tier" was five acts across two screens with a human wait in the middle, and the decision behind it was recorded nowhere. `given` is that decision as an append-only row: an address, a plan × N workspaces or a number of credits, an optional term, a required reason, and the operator who signed it. It is made to an ADDRESS because a demo, a friend and a cash customer have usually never signed in; `upsertAccount` adopts what was written for them. A plan gift confers the right to found — counted WITH the bare commercial allowance, or an operator would have to raise a second number and forgetting refuses somebody the thing they were just given. `applyGifts` is the one application path and both doors call it: founding, and an operator applying to a workspace somebody already has. The plan and the allowance land in the same instant rather than on tomorrow's sweep; the gift's term travels onto the subscription so the nightly pass can end it, because bounding only the SPENDING would give a year of cash the tier for ever. And the workspace can tell: `money.view` carries `given`, so the shelf says "Given, and free until the first of December" where it printed a price over a card that does not exist. Two silent faults fell out — `topUp` and `grantAllowance` wrote a ledger line and an `UPDATE` that matched nothing on a workspace whose billing account was never opened, and one draft comped under the caller's app id while `renewAllowance` reads `MEMBERSHIP`, so the plan landed and the allowance was zero. Accounts and one account are console screens; no Stripe is in any of it. D48.

stages.title: A browser test does not gate a deploy
stages.ends: The CI job downloaded Chromium and its system libraries, then waited on twelve suites that render the shipped stylesheet and measure pixels — 97 seconds in the design package alone, 96 of them one file, more than every guard, typecheck and runtime suite put together. None of what they ask is what a deploy is waiting on: they answer whether a screen LOOKS right, and a deploy is asking whether the thing answers at all. They are `*.seen.test.*` now, excluded from every `test` config and run by `pnpm engine:seen`, which nothing in CI calls — so the cost is paid by whoever is changing a screen. Design's fast lane went 97s to 8s and the workflow installs no browser. The whole arrangement is a filename, which is why `scripts/seen.test.mjs` exists: it fails on a browser suite without the suffix, a suffixed suite that opens none, a package holding one with no `seen` script, a `test` config whose globs still pick one up — evaluated against the real filenames rather than read for the word `seen` — and a workflow that installs a browser again. `docs/guards.json` gained a `lane` field, because four registered guards are no longer reached by CI and a registry saying otherwise is worse than none. D49.

stages.title: Ambient motion is earned, and a field has a budget
stages.ends: The world's marks beat in SMIL inside a `<pattern>`, which is the only thing that repaints in one — and a repaint inside a paint server invalidates the whole fill, so every frame re-rasterised a tile and repainted a viewport-sized rect on the main thread, for as long as a screen was open, competing with scrolling. Measured at the density a list screen asks for: the fine lattice was 2,820 placements, 394 live animations and 504 KB of markup; the line-art family 432 and 10. `motionFor` is the one decision now, from a stored choice and what the device says about itself, and it answers in two tiers — ESSENTIAL motion (arrival, travel, a press, a chart drawing: short, one-shot, composited, and carrying meaning) is assumed, AMBIENT motion (endless, full-screen, never composited) is EARNED. A fine pointer is the entry condition because a mid-range phone reports eight cores and cannot report a mouse; memory and cores only veto, and their silence is not a refusal. `useStillness` became a projection of it rather than a second answer. The other half is the cost that a motion setting cannot reach: a still field is still a string to parse and a tree to rasterise, so `MARKS` caps what a field may emit and the TILE shrinks rather than the cell — the same picture repeating sooner, against half a megabyte on every screen. Measured after: 588 placements, 133 KB, and no live animations on the default path. And the switch is reachable at last: every keyframe answered `data-reduce-motion` and nothing set it, `applyAppearance` read a value nothing wrote — `Look and motion` is both, on the device rather than the account, and it says which fact about the hardware decided. D50.

stages.title: A workspace is founded with the products somebody chose
stages.ends: `me.tenant.create` founded with `apps: [deps.appId]` and `deps.appId` was the string `"hello"`, hardcoded in the worker — so every workspace anybody made held the reference app whatever they came for, and the only way to change it afterwards was to ask an operator to do it in the console. A deployment that serves several products and can only hand out the first is one product with the others built. Founding takes the ids now, narrowed to a `sells` catalogue that is deliberately a separate list from what is SERVED — a product mid-build stays mounted for the workspaces an operator put it in and comes out of one line — and refuses an empty choice, because a workspace with no product is a name and an address with nothing to open. `me.products` reads the manifests so the wizard cannot hold a second catalogue that goes stale, and `app.list`/`app.add`/`app.remove` let an owner change it later, with the last one un-removable: a workspace with nothing on cannot reach the screen that would switch something back on. Switching one on is a row and nothing else, because every product's schema is applied to every shard at boot. The first name for those three was `product.*`, which SILENTLY REPLACED OneInventory's own `product.list` — platform operations are merged over an app's generated CRUD on purpose — so `compose` refuses a shadowing id outright now instead of resolving it. D51. The screen is `Apps` under a workspace — `apps` rather than `products` because `packages` one row up is what the workspace SELLS, and two rows a word apart meaning opposite sides of the same trade is a menu somebody has to open to tell apart. Adding one also grants the person who did it the app's FOUNDING ROLE: enabling a product is a directory row saying the workspace HAS it, not that anybody may open one, so without that the owner presses the switch and every route in the new product answers 403 to them. Them alone — a grant nobody made is not made here — and `canAssign` is bypassed at that one point on purpose, because nobody holds a key in a product switched on a moment ago and the ordinary rule would make the first role in any new product ungrantable for ever.

stages.title: The ground is a fixture, and the deployment serves no fixture
stages.ends: The smallest complete app on the engine — one notebook, sample content, every cross-cutting concern declared so the framework's claims are asserted against something real — was in the deployment's `APPS`, in its `SELLS`, and in the browser's product loader. So a person who came for one product founded a workspace holding a demo they never asked for, with somebody else's notes in it, and only an operator could take it away. Nobody decided that; it was where the fixture happened to live. It is `engine/ground` now, outside `engine/apps` — which is the product catalogue — and the rule is structural rather than an exemption: `fixture.test.mjs` asks whether anything the deployment serves comes from outside the catalogue, which is a fact about a path rather than a claim about one app. Its `live` half, the entry that drew its screens over a workspace's own records, is deleted: a fixture with a live browser half is a product nobody decided to sell. The dev-only ground PAGE stays, because `import.meta.env.DEV` folds it out of the bundle and `bundle.test.mjs` holds that. What the deployment's own suite proves moved with the products: `boot`, `dossier` and `agent` drive OneInventory now, and what inventory cannot express — an app's own retention rule, two products to switch between — moved to the ground's suite, where a fixture can declare anything. The move also narrowed twenty guards at once, silently, because each enumerated `engine/apps/*` by hand and the ground had been inside it; `lib/trees.mjs` is the one walk they all read now, and widening `settings` back over the ground found `notes.density` saved and read by nothing the moment its only reader was deleted. Two defects came out of driving it: `app.add` answered 200 when the enablement never landed — a switch that snaps on over a product whose every route is 404 — and the sub-processor register disclosed `sensitive` to the company running the databases when no mounted app collects any. D52.

stages.title: The navigation is five destinations, and the chrome carries the rest
stages.ends: OneInventory declared five primary destinations and eight secondary ones, and the secondary tier WAS navigation: the desktop rail listed it and the phone spent the fifth of its five slots on an item that opened a sheet of the rest. Thirteen places to look, a bar that could not answer "where am I" from eight of them, and the same product reading differently either side of the breakpoint. The ceiling was never the problem — the overflow was, and a ceiling with an overflow behind it is not a ceiling. `nav` is `"primary" | "none"` now, the first destination is the app's own root, and the chrome has two named slots an app declares into: `chrome: "search"` takes the crown's middle, which used to hold the workspace name — a question nobody was asking, in the widest slot a working screen has — and `chrome: "assistant"` is a button beside the notifications, because asking is something somebody does FROM a screen about what is on it. A screen claiming a slot AND a bar seat is refused at composition. Where a screen's one act goes falls out of the same fact: a destination's foot is the navigation so the act rides up to the crown, and a screen somebody WENT to has no bar, so the act takes that room — never both, which was `Docked`'s own rule. Neither end is a bar: both are the page's ground with a hem, and the desktop rail was the last plate left — a column of filled buttons against ink on a phone — so it wears the bar's own `data-island` treatment and pins under the crown. Moving between screens stopped rebuilding the world: `worldCss` places up to `MARKS` marks and ran on every render, so a poll landing handed React several hundred fresh marks under a page that was often also changing, which is what made travel read as the app reloading. And the six screens that left the bar were reached from nowhere for one commit — declared, mounted, rendering perfectly, openable only by typing — so `reached.test.mjs` asks every app whether a screen off the bar has a control that leads to it, matching the router handoff rather than the route's name, because every container carries the mount table and a check on the string passes over an app whose every control has been unwired. D53.

stages.title: A home screen, and a checklist that knows whose step it is
stages.ends:
OneInventory opened on Stock — a page of rows somebody has to read to find out whether there is anything to do — and had no screen answering "is everything all right". Home is the root now: what is on the shelf as one figure, the four acts the bar does not already hold (receiving, labels, the spreadsheet, the suppliers — a shortcut to something a thumb reaches from every screen is a second answer to one question), what is waiting with a count each, the checklist while it is unfinished, and the movements cut down to what a first screen holds with the way on to Reports underneath. Stock moved to `/stock` and Reports gave up its bar seat, because most of its figures are on Home already and a seat for a screen that is another screen's summary is the bar answering "where am I" with two places that are the same place. The four entries stage 81d put on Stock went with it; the spreadsheet stayed, because it is the only one of them that is a way of filling THAT list and on the first morning it is the only way anybody fills it at all.

The engine half is the checklist itself, and it was wrong for half of every workspace. The guide was derived entirely from `tenant_event`, the workspace-wide tally — right for setup, wrong for everything a pair of hands has to learn — so somebody invited into a workspace that had been running opened a checklist already complete: every box crossed off by their employer, nothing taught, and nothing failing anywhere, because the list simply rendered empty and read as success. `StepDef.who` is `"workspace" | "person"` now, absent meaning the workspace so a book written before the axis keeps its meaning; `Raised` carries both lists and a step is looked up on the axis it declares, never a union. The personal record is a yes rather than a tally — `person_event`, one row per person per event, written the first time and never again, narrowed at the write to the events some step actually names — so what is kept about a member is which of their own first steps they have taken and a product declaring no person step keeps no personal row at all. D54.

One thing came out of photographing it that no static check could see: the nav's closed labels are held at zero width with an ellipsis on them, so the geometry sweep read four "cut" words in every bar in the product. The trim belongs to the open label and to nothing else.

stages.title: A product's colour is the product's, and one family commits
stages.ends:
Two changes and they are the same change. First: `AppSpec.hue` — a product declares one OKLCH value and `Page` sets it as `--brand` on the element the ground is painted on, which is what every family reads its `lit` slot from, so the ground, the source in it, the wash on every surface and the halo under a heading are one line. A design is a set of relationships somebody chose, and while the colour arrived from a workspace's picker no screen could be designed because no screen knew what it would be made of.

Second: `neon`, and it is the first family that commits. Every world before it was quiet — right, and why a product's rich screens land at all — and none of them could make the screen somebody opens the app onto feel like anything, because a ground is BEHIND the page and the card on top of it stays the grey it is on a screen with no world. A hard bright SOURCE on black, a ring far larger than the frame or a beam, with an almost-white core and the hue living in the falloff. Its peak is not opaque, because a band at full alpha erases whatever it passes over and on a phone that is a heading; a beam's hot point keeps out of the middle, which is the one placement rule the family does not leave to the seed, because the middle of a beam's axis is where a home screen puts its one figure.

`Family.wash` is the half every other family leaves out — a second, louder colour that SURFACES are made of, published as `--scene-wash` and mixed into the tiers by one rule in the stylesheet. Seven of the eight decline; the rules select on an attribute set only where a family published one, so nothing is half-washed by a fallback. The share rises with the tier, because washing a page, a card and a control by the same amount collapses three tiers into one flat field. And the hue goes in whole: amber mixed toward black is brown, and a card washed in brown reads as dirty rather than as lit.

The motion rule turned out to be "not under the blend" rather than "nothing moves". The grain is `mix-blend-mode`, so anything animating below it re-blends a viewport-sized stack sixty times a second — which is what killed the ground's old drift, and is a property of where a layer sits. `Ground.flare` is the family's own split: the shallow bloom stays under the dither where the grain stops it banding, and the steep band goes above it, on its own layer, where a rotation of a degree and a half over ninety seconds is compositor-only and costs one promoted layer. Earned from the same budget the beats answer to, and off both ways.

OneInventory takes amber and puts Home on it, and Home's hero floats: no title, no strapline, no card. Nobody navigates to home — they arrive there, the crown already says where they are, and what goes in the space a heading would have taken is the number they opened the app for. D55.

stages.title: A design rule is a guard, and the measuring is done in a browser
stages.ends:
The interface language was a document, and a document is advice. Four rules came in from outside and became checks — `transition: all`, an ungated `:hover`, a keyword easing curve, and a chart package setting seven type sizes for three jobs — and four more were rejected in writing rather than left as silence somebody re-argues (D70). What the browser reading found is the part no source-reading check could have: ink is a measurement, not a token name. Sixty-one contrast faults across nineteen screens in both themes, the worst of them a chemical-hazard sentence at 1.94:1, all of them a status colour tuned as a FILL being used as text — and the fix was found by rendering every candidate between 30% and 90% and measuring, not by taste. Two of the harness's own readings were wrong first and reported perfect screens: `slice.call` on a Map's iterator returns an empty array, so every screen reported no type at all; and the contrast parser assumed `rgb()` while Chromium answers in the author's colour space, so white on black measured 1.00. A palette fix then measured worse than the fault — `--muted: color-mix(… var(--muted) …)` on `body` is a CSS cycle and the browser discards the property, which resolved light-mode muted to pure black: it passed the floor while destroying the token's whole purpose, and only re-measuring caught it.

Two mechanisms went with it. `Outcome` is required on every write now — fifteen of fifty operations said nothing at all when they worked — and the exemption is a sentence rather than a flag, because a `silent: true` is a box somebody ticks (D71). And `problem` stopped being bypassable: `PickFile` had written its own three refusals in the file that draws them, in a colour measured at 3.39:1, so a file rejected in the browser read in different words and a different tone from the same file rejected by the server.

The last finding is the one that says why any of this is done in a browser. Thirty-nine screens — the operator console and the account centre, the surfaces with the most controls per page in this deployment — were in no sweep at all, and the sweep written for them found `/space/data` rendering nothing: a white page in production, from six characters. `slot="trigger"` is correct on a `Disclosure` and correct in a fixture, and inside a presented surface it is resolved against the enclosing `Modal`, which offers `close` and throws. The design package's own mounted test carried the same fault and passed, because nothing encloses a component mounted alone.

The reading written to catch that fault then found a second one, which is the argument for a browser in one sentence: `Peek` wrapped its `Button` in `Popover.Trigger`, and react-aria put a `div role="button" tabindex="0"` around it carrying the SAME `id`. Two tab stops for one control, "button, button" to a screen reader, and a duplicate name under the popover's own `aria-*` wiring — which resolves by `getElementById` and therefore takes whichever came first. Every existing reading passed over it: the box was the right size, the ink cleared the floor, the page did not spill. `Geometry.twins` is that probe kept, asserted on every screen in the deployment, and it carries exactly one exemption — HeroUI's `DateField.Group` and `DateField.Input` both render `role="group"` with the field's id, reproduced from the library's own documented anatomy with nothing of ours in the tree. It is written as a SHAPE rather than a count, so a third element on the same name still fails, and it can only shrink.

And one fixture was found to be racing the question it exists to answer: `world.seen` grew the page on a timer and read "did it start short?" as soon as the hem appeared, so on a loaded machine it failed on its own precondition. Green when fast, red when busy, which teaches a reader to re-run rather than to look. The test pulls the trigger now instead of waiting for one.

stages.title: The bar earns its material: bespoke marks, one lit destination, one movement
stages.ends:
Four items were reported as a bug and were not one — five are declared and `Work` is withheld from that workspace because its plan does not include processes, which `centre-ops` does deliberately and for a written reason: a withheld destination is ABSENT rather than locked, since the alternative is a nav row that offers something and then apologises. What WAS wrong is everything around it.

Three of the four marks meant something else. Home was a star, which means favourite; Scan was a magnifier, which means somebody looking for a thing they cannot see rather than a machine reading one in their hand; Count was a double-check, which is the mark on a delivered message — put on the screen somebody opens to START a count. `home` already existed in the registry and was not being used. `scan` and `tally` did not exist at all, so both are drawn now, in the same 24×24 hand as the library with their moving parts named: a viewfinder whose beam sweeps, and a tally whose crossing stroke is drawn. The tally is THREE uprights rather than the literal four, and that is a size decision found by rendering it — five strokes across sixteen pixels puts the gaps narrower than the ink and the mark reads as hatching.

The switch had never animated. `MOTION.reveal` names `max-height` and the bar animates `max-width`, so for as long as the compact bar has existed the label's width has SNAPPED and only its opacity moved — under a header describing a word that grows out of one item while the one before it closes. `unfold` and `fold` are two intents rather than one, because the asymmetry is the effect: the outgoing word is quicker, so the room is free before anything moves into it.

And the bar had no material at all. It carries no fill by design — every plate and pill was removed, each for a measured reason — which left four grey glyphs and one white one on the page's own ground. The active item is now LIT rather than filled: a halo of the product's own `--brand` under the glyph, at two strengths because a warm mix adds luminance on black and subtracts it on cream, where one strength came out looking like highlighter. Under the glyph and nowhere near the word, because the contrast reading composites every translucent layer above text.

Two things about how this was found are worth keeping. The ceiling that keeps the closed items from sprawling was written, typechecked and did nothing until the SPA was rebuilt — Tailwind emits only the utilities it has SEEN, so a class added to a token file does not exist until the compiler reads it, which is invisible to every check over TypeScript. And the light disappeared entirely in the first fixture because the hue was passed as an OKLCH triple rather than a colour: `color-mix` on an invalid value drops the whole declaration, and nothing else about the bar changes. Both are assertions now.

stages.title: A model is given something to hear, and the seconds are counted before they are spent
A wizard narrates: one question a screen, and what you answered stays said
stages.ends: The register sheet was four headings over groups of fields, and the field under the third of them — the tracking rung, which decides what a person is asked at every future delivery — was four bare words with four explanations written beside them that reached nobody: it was a `Segmented`, and `Segmented` renders `o.label` and nothing else. Its own header says segments are for a choice worn on the surface and never for data entry. `Story` is the general answer: an `Ask` is a question, its controls, and the CLAUSE its answer makes — one string doing two jobs, the live echo under the control and the line in the recap, so they cannot drift. The recap doubles as navigation, which is what turns checking a model's twenty filled fields into reading eight sentences. Three things came out of building it. The pure `walk` found a real bug on its second test: the last step's own refusal was drawn as a row navigating to a DIFFERENT step, because the way-there was taken from the first owing step regardless of which branch supplied the sentence. The packing clause was rewritten by measurement rather than taste — "A box holds 10 sheets, and a sheet holds 10 tablets — 100 tablets in a box" is correct, readable and seventeen words, which on a phone is a recap row wrapping three times; "A box of 10 sheets of 10 tablets" is the same fact in the form a distributor already says it in. And the new guard found bugs in itself first, twice: `ask:` matched the proving ground's sample data, where it is a column meaning who asked and every value is an email address, and `step={` matched a number field's increment.

stages.title: The interface stops looking like a fintech: warm material, one hot mark, generous corners
The declared surface — the contract
stages.ends:
The line was never a principle. Eleven surfaces are already drawn from declarations no app writes a line of — settings, the money pages, the console, the policy reader, the vault sheet, the guide, the field editor — and what was left hand-written is a PRODUCT's own screens, which is simply where the work stopped. This is the contract that closes it: `ScreenSpec` grows an `of` and a `body`, `AppSpec` grows `views`, and a screen becomes something the kernel can refuse.

The design is one decision repeated: every expression is a CLOSED SET and there is no operator anywhere. A value is read from one of five places, wears one of seven named formatters, and is tested for presence and nothing else. A comparison, a sum or a threshold is not expressible on purpose — it becomes a query on the collection, where it is typed, tested, and read the same way by everything else that reads that collection. That is an escape VALVE rather than a hatch: a hatch takes the logic somewhere nothing can see it, and the valve pushes it down into the data layer where the kernel already refuses a field that is not there.

Fourteen refusals, and every one of them draws a page today rather than throwing: a block nothing registers, a block that has not implemented all four states, a slot given a kind of source it cannot draw, a required slot left unbound, a field bound on a screen that is about nothing, a formatter that will say `Invalid Date`, a view narrowing on a column that does not exist, a span wider than its grid. The sharpest is the field with no subject — every binding resolves to undefined, and a heading bound to undefined is a blank line, so the screen reads as unfinished rather than broken and survives review.

Two things the writing settled. `ScreenShape` had two copies, and only one of them was consulted by `SHAPES`, the preset table that decides a page's width, its skeleton and where its one action goes — so a declared shape the table had never heard of would not throw, it would fall through and draw a settings page as a form. It is the kernel's now and the design package aliases it. And `kernel/src/blocks.ts` ships EMPTY, refusing every block: a screen may not name what nothing registers, and an index that let unknown names through would be worse than no index at all, because the failure would then be a blank region in production instead of a refusal at composition.

stages.title: The spike: the three hardest screens, and the easy one that was mistaken for the general case
stages.ends:
Register, Receive and Scan expressed against the contract with no renderer and no way out, and none of the three can be expressed. That is the correct answer at stage 90 and would have been an expensive one at 96.

The plan said "25 screens, 10,130 lines" as though they were one kind of thing. Measured, they are three: twelve READS with no state, no effects and no capture at all (2,829 lines); two files of WIRING that are not screens (3,518); and eleven that CAPTURE, holding unsaved answers before a write (3,783). The sample the plan reasoned from was one of the twelve — the easy case mistaken for the general one, which is the failure a spike exists to catch.

Two things were missing and only one was a gap. Presence could ask whether there was a code and not what the code TURNED OUT TO BE, which is what three of these screens are: a scanned label that is a shelf sends the session there, a known product is a thing to open, an unknown one is a question — three cards and three acts behind one action. `Presence` gained one arm, and it stays closed because it may only be asked of an `enum`: the field has declared its values, so a branch on one the column can never hold is refused as a card nobody will ever see, and a dispatch over free text is refused as the comparison it is. Anything else becomes an enum on the collection, the same direction a derived field goes.

The second was not a gap. Receive holds four answers re-seeded per scan and computes a pack multiplier the server also computes; Register holds twenty-four pieces of state and narrates each as a clause. Nothing declarative should express that and the framework already said so — `story` exists, Register already is one, and its own header draws the line where it belongs. So the taxonomy went into the contract rather than being discovered at the port: a screen is a body or a story, and a screen carrying both is refused, because a renderer would otherwise pick one silently by whichever it checked first.

And the largest finding was not in the three screens. `live.tsx` is 2,579 lines — a quarter of the app — and is not a screen: it fetches, joins and hands props, and its own header argues for a declared query by name while explaining why it could not have one. That container, not the screens, is the biggest single thing this arc removes.

One thing the writing settled on its own: the walk that takes a `when` apart existed twice, once for views and once for fields, and adding the new arm meant editing both. Whichever was missed would have gone on reporting green about a conditional it could no longer see. It is one function now.

stages.title: The block registry: forty blocks, counted rather than surveyed
stages.ends:
Forty blocks, and the set was chosen by tallying what the twelve reading screens actually draw rather than by surveying what the design package exports. Rows first, because a row of some kind is drawn more often across those screens than every other block put together.

The membership is DERIVED and the meaning is DECLARED, which is not what the plan promised and is the honest shape. `scripts/vocabulary.test.mjs` reads the design package's source and refuses both ways: an entry naming a component that is not exported, and a component that could be a block and is classified as nothing. A candidate is any exported component taking no `children` — `children` means the caller composes, and a declaration cannot — so all 192 are a block or are named in one of seven categories with a reason, and those lists can only shrink. What no generator could derive is what a slot MEANS: "the rows" against "how many", and that this one takes a view and nothing else. A `React.ReactNode` says none of that, and a generator that guessed would be inventing the answer.

Three changes to the contract came out of building it. A body nests exactly one level, because `Section` and `Group` are the two most-drawn components in the product by a wide margin and the flat contract would have made every screen one undivided column; a group holds blocks and never another group, since one level is a layout and two is a tree. The four outcomes moved to the FRAME rather than into forty components — the registry made it plain that almost none of them implement any today, and building them in would be thirty-nine copies of one decision, which is the shape this whole arc exists to remove; a block declares its skeleton and the frame draws the rest, which turns stage 93 from forty pieces of work into one. And `goes` was added, because half the rows in a product navigate and `does` could only name an operation; it names a SCREEN rather than a route, so a row that leads nowhere is refused instead of being the one fault that reads as a slow app.

The guard found bugs in itself before it found any in the tree, twice. Its first parser read an argument list with a lazy regex, which stops at the first `)` inside a destructured default or a generic — so five real components, every row spreading `RowBase` plus the generic `Listing`, were reported as missing from the design package. A guard whose parser is wrong reports the tree as broken and is believed. And it counted SCREAMING_CASE constants as components. The second finding was in the engine: naming the skeleton field `waiting` collided with a count called `waiting` in the console, and the closed-set guard began reporting a number as an enum drawn as words. It is `bones` now, which is what the design package already calls a skeleton.

stages.title: A block reflows by its own measured box, and the screen is held still to prove it
stages.ends:
A block reflows by the box it was given, and a breakpoint is a claim about the screen that a block has no business making. `Listing` collapsed on `md:` — right while a list is always the width of the page, wrong the moment one sits in a cell of a board: on a 1440px monitor the viewport says "wide", so four columns are drawn into 300 pixels and every one of them is a word per line. The reverse costs as much, and a list given the whole of a 700px tablet stays a phone list. This is also the rule that makes a declared layout possible at all, and the reason a `Span` is what the layout is told rather than what the block reads: a block told what slot it is in works in the layouts using that vocabulary and breaks in every one that does not, including the ones nobody has designed yet.

`BOX` and `ROOM` in `metrics.ts` are the mechanism, at one threshold — the width a table of real words actually needs — and every class is written out whole rather than interpolated, because Tailwind emits only what it has SEEN and `${AT.wide}:hidden` would exist in TypeScript and in no stylesheet. That is the same silence that left a whole token file inert until the SPA was rebuilt.

The guard found a second instance nobody had looked for: `SubProcessors` in `legal.tsx` had the identical collapse, on a disclosure whose own comment argues at length why four columns in a phone's width is not a table — so a compliance table drawn in one column of a two-column page got the four-column layout because the MONITOR was wide.

And the measured half is what no static check could do. A breakpoint and a container query are indistinguishable in every reading that VARIES the window: both collapse a list on a phone and open it on a desk, so a sweep at two viewport widths reports success either way. `reflowOf` holds the viewport at 1440 and gives the block three boxes, reading which parts were actually LAID OUT rather than which are in the document — both halves of a collapse are always in the markup, one of them `display:none`. The middle reading, 400 pixels inside a 1440 pixel window, is the single measurement that separates the two mechanisms.

Two other guards had to be widened rather than waived, and both were right to fire. `heroui` refused `@2xl:grow-0` as a restyle because its prefix pattern only knew the viewport spelling — so obeying D92 failed the guard that protects D7. And `present` read `${ROOM.until}` as a stored date drawn unformatted, because `until` is a date-shaped field name in the kernel; the token is `ROOM.narrow` and `ROOM.wide` now, which is better English than what it replaced. The new guard also found a bug in itself first: its comment filter matched a `*` down the left edge, which a JSX `{/* … */}` block does not have, so the middle of the paragraph explaining why a button is `h-10 md:h-9` was reported as a violation of the rule it was explaining.

stages.title: The four outcomes are the frame's, and what a block owes is the shape of its own absence
stages.ends:
The four outcomes are drawn once, around whichever block the frame is placing, using the skeleton that block declares. Stage 91 is what made this one small: building waiting, nothing, trouble and denied into forty components would have been thirty-nine copies of one decision, which is the shape the whole arc exists to remove.

`nothing` is a REQUIRED field, and that is most of the component. Every surface that rendered an empty array as a confident fact did so because saying what emptiness MEANS was something a caller could leave out — a passkey card showing a "0" badge for the length of a round trip, a bell saying "you're all caught up" mid-fetch, a media library whose `catch` turned a failed load into "no media yet". A field nobody has to fill is a field that stays empty; a required one is how that stops being a thing to remember.

Denied comes first, which is deliberately not the order `Await` uses. The other three are about a request and this one is about whether there should be a request at all — so a skeleton followed by a refusal is a promise the screen breaks a second later, and it is worse than the refusal on its own because somebody has already started waiting for it. The rest of the order is `Await`'s and is not arbitrary: trouble outranks emptiness, because a failed request has no data and `[]` is what a naive reading of it produces; waiting outranks both, because during the round trip neither is known yet.

Three call sites moved over, each of which had been wiring the same three by hand. The ones that did not are the line worth writing down: a screen whose answer can never legitimately be empty — the plan catalogue, the maintenance modes — keeps `Await`, because a required "what emptiness means" on a list that is never empty is a sentence nobody will ever read and somebody has to invent.

stages.title: The layouts: relationships rather than breakpoints
stages.ends:
Three arrangements, not four. The board folded into the grid — a board is a grid of tiles, and the only thing separating the two declarations was how wide a cell may be, which is a field.

A COLUMN COUNT IS A SLOT COORDINATE ONE LEVEL UP, and it had to go the same way stage 92 sent the breakpoints. `{ as: "grid", cols: 3 }` names a number that is right at exactly one width; every other width needs a breakpoint to correct it, which is the thing stage 92 spent itself removing from the blocks. A layout that reintroduces one at the frame has moved the fault rather than fixed it. It is `least: "tile" | "panel" | "card"` now — the narrowest a cell may be, with `auto-fit` deciding how many fit — and `Grid`'s own header had been making that argument for months while the layout contract went the other way. The same edit ran through `split`, whose `lead: number` percentage became `aside: "start" | "end"` (which side it is DRAWN on, the reading order fixed, because putting a filter panel before the results because it is drawn on the left is how a page becomes unusable without being wrong), and through `Span`, whose `cols` became `cells`.

`beside: true` is how a block claims the aside, and both directions refuse. A split where nothing claims it does not fail: it draws one column and an empty gutter, which reads as a screen that loaded half of itself. Two claims is the same fault from the other end — the second silently replaces the first.

AND THE MEASUREMENT FOUND A REGRESSION STAGE 92 HAD INTRODUCED. `Columns` and `Segmented` each carried the container declaration and the rule that queries it on the SAME element. An element cannot query itself, so both rules were inert at every width: the declaration typechecked, the classes were emitted into the stylesheet, and the columns never separated. The reflow guard's "every file that queries a box also declares one" was satisfied, because the file did declare one — the check was about files and the fault was about elements. Only asking a browser how many columns actually came out could see it, which is the same reason stage 92 needed a browser at all. Both are wrappers now and the guard has a fourth check that reads the class string rather than the file.

The reading itself is four questions a static check cannot ask: a stack draws one column, a grid draws more than one, tiles fit more across than cards at the same width (which is what makes the closed set of cell widths mean anything rather than being three names for one number), and a split's aside sits beside its main column with the main column still stacked. The aside is found by its tag and its previous sibling rather than by DOM depth — a reading that counts levels breaks on the correct fix and passes on the incorrect one, which is exactly the trap the wrapper had just set.

stages.title: The guards, re-founded on the schema
stages.ends:
The plan said sixty-nine source-scanning guards would become schema-scanning guards. It is fifty-six that sweep a product — measured — and almost none of them can be re-pointed. A guard keyed on a `className`, a `<Card`, a bare `fetch` or a `catch` that answers a failure with a fact cannot ask its question of a `body:`, because the declaration has no such clause. The question does not convert; it DISSOLVES, and a dissolved question and an unasked one look identical from outside.

A PORTED SCREEN DOES NOT FAIL A GUARD. IT STOPS BEING ASKED. Nothing turns red — the corpus just gets smaller, one screen at a time, and a guard printing `ok` over forty files reads exactly like a guard printing `ok` over sixty. That is the fault `lib/trees.mjs` already exists for, where one directory move took the proving ground out of twenty sweeps at once, except this time it is scheduled and deliberate and spread over three stages, which makes it harder to notice rather than easier.

So the answer is written down per guard BEFORE the port, in the registry, and there are five: the kernel refuses it (checked — the code must be in the refusal union and a kernel test must assert it), the grammar has no clause for it, the guard reads declarations itself (checked — it must import the reader), the question never depended on a screen being a FILE, or it is about a story's controls, which stay in the app. The two that cannot be checked mechanically must carry their reason in the same string, so that saying them is an act in a diff rather than a silence.

ZERO `reads` IS THE RESULT, AND IT WAS NOT THE EXPECTED ONE. The stage was scoped expecting a pile of guards needing to be re-pointed at the manifest; there are none. Every question either dissolves in the grammar or already lives somewhere a body lands inside — the manifest, the runtime, the design package. The declared surface does not open a coverage hole. The ledger is what establishes that instead of assuming it, and the seventeen `unrepresentable` claims are the list the renderer has to not violate.

The sharpest single answer is `keys`, whose own header calls its subject the most-repeated fault in this product: a screen printing a machine key where a name belongs. Declared, it stops being a screen's fault at all and becomes the field's — `labels` on the enum, named once for every screen that will ever draw it. Asking it at the field found five live ones, all shipping: a picker offering "Gtin", "Gs1", "Ai-assisted" and "Ok", because sentence case has only the key to go on and is right to sentence-case it. Re-founding a question moved it from the rendering site, where it is asked once per screen and only where somebody wrote one, to the declaration, where it is asked once and covers every screen including the ones nobody has written.

AND THE READER IS ASKED WHETHER IT CAN STILL SEE. All of this rests on a text read of `screens: [` in each manifest, which is the one kind of check that answers `none` rather than throwing when the shape moves under it — so an app contributing no screens is a failure rather than a number. Both halves of that were found by mutation rather than by reasoning: the first draft under-counted thirty-one screens as six because its detector looked for a field a screen does not carry, and the refusal check passed a deliberately renamed code because `includes` is a substring test and the rename left the old name inside the new one.

stages.title: The renderer: a screen is drawn from what it declares
stages.ends:
A screen is drawn from what it declares, end to end: the proving ground's Notes screen names a `Listing`, binds it to a declared view, and the door hands back the rows. Nothing in `engine/ground/src/screens` draws it.

THE RENDERER WAS NOT THE BLOCKED PART. The registry that stood between a declaration and a component had been documentation of an imagined API — twenty-three of forty slots named a prop the component does not take — and React drops an unknown prop without a word, so binding `rows` to a `Listing` that reads `of` composes, mounts, typechecks and draws a table with a header and no rows. Every check in the repository was blind to it, because every check read the registry rather than a rendered tree. `vocabulary.test.mjs` asks the static half now (is this slot a prop the component takes) and `design/test/body.test.tsx` watches a distinctive value come out of the far end. Thirteen charts went in the same pass — they were listed rather than counted, and they do not share one API, so what shipped is the two that do.

AND THE SERVER SIDE WAS BLOCKED BELOW THE SURFACE: nothing served `AppSpec.views` at all. The order it forced is the one that held — the runner, then the composer, then the route, then the first declaration, each unwritable without the one before it. `runViews` runs a screen's views in one round trip because a screen's regions each wait on their own outcome in the browser, and N sequential queries behind one door would put every region behind the slowest.

THE PERMISSION IS THE COLLECTION'S, AND THAT IS THE ONE THAT MATTERS. A screen carries a `permission` for whether it is OFFERED; this door hands back ROWS, and the permission governing a row is its collection's. Checking the screen's alone lets a `stock` screen with a supplier listing on it hand supplier rows to somebody who may not read suppliers — a manifest anybody could write, which composes, with every suite green. It is derived by calling the kernel's own `permissionFor(spec, "read")` rather than by spelling the prefix rule a second time, which is how the first draft got it wrong. And it refuses WHOLE rather than serving the part the caller may: dropping the views somebody cannot read draws a screen with a region missing, which reads as a workspace with no suppliers rather than as an account that cannot see them, and the person acts on the first reading.

WHAT A BLOCK OWES IS THE SHAPE OF ITS OWN ABSENCE, and the words are the app's. Each block waits on the view IT reads and nothing else, so a heading and a note are not held behind the slowest list on the page. `nothing` is required of any block that reads a list — the kernel refuses `nothing_unsaid` — because a renderer inventing "Nothing here yet" is every empty list in every product saying the same nothing, with the app taken out of the loop.

The door closes: no private UI in an app
